source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
source.authors: Hoagy Cunningham; Aidan Ewart; L. Smith; R. Huben; Lee Sharkey

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse dictionary learning to language-model activations and reports interpretability and causal-localisation results, extending superposition-related claims to language models.
record.gate_note: The study reports outcomes for sparse-autoencoder features in language models, including comparisons with other decompositions, feature ablations, and reconstruction quality. Hyperparameter values used to train the dictionaries are not separate results.
record.test_reason: The study trains sparse autoencoders on Pythia residual-stream and MLP activations. It reports whether recoverable sparse, interpretable, causally relevant features exist (V4), and reports reconstruction loss and a smooth sparsity tradeoff that bear on completeness and canonicity (V5). It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors also claim SAEs are a scalable, unsupervised way to resolve superposition in language models, and that the features are more monosemantic than comparable methods. Their stated limits are reconstruction loss and MLP overcompleteness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders to learn dictionaries from language-model activations, then evaluates interpretability and causal localisation; it does not reproduce the original toy-model experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability advantage varies by layer and is weaker in later layers. Results also depend on scoring protocol (top-and-random versus random-only), sparsity coefficient, and activation type (residual stream versus MLP).

fits_no_version.finding: Interpretability scores correlate weakly with skew and kurtosis of feature activations (about 0.15–0.24).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Heavy-tailed (non-Gaussian) activation directions are more interpretable.

record.problems: The study acknowledges nonzero reconstruction loss and increased perplexity when reconstructed activations replace the original activations. MLP results are mixed, with many dead features. Several comparisons are presented as plots without numerical values in the text; individual qualitative case studies do not establish broad feature completeness or stability.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity phase transition or feature geometry.
No test of importance versus capacity allocation.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity tested.
Stability of features across seeds, data or checkpoints, and cross-run canonicity, are not tested.
Features are assumed to be 1-D directions. Multi-dimensional features are not tested.

missing.what: Interpretability advantage holds even for undercomplete dictionaries (R<1), so it is not tied to overcompleteness.
Top-K PCA/ICA control explains only a small fraction of the SAE advantage.
MLP SAE features are more interpretable than neurons (top-and-random and random-only scores).
Residual dictionaries stay at least 4x overcomplete before features drop out.
IOI patching results on layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and 23 of Pythia-410M.
Residual-stream basis directions are no more interpretable than random directions.

record.verdict_notes: Most evidence is figure-only, without numeric values in the text. The V5 verdict uses limits_scope rather than the record's 'challenges', because the uniqueness evidence is explicitly hedged and incompleteness is partial rather than absent.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular feature geometry are not experimentally tested.
The study does not test whether importance determines which features get dedicated dimensions versus shared capacity.
It does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
The study does not establish that its dictionaries recover all features, or assess feature spread across neurons across a broad range of models.
Completeness and uniqueness are addressed in part; stability of feature identities across seeds, data, or checkpoints is not tested.
The study represents dictionary features as directions but does not test whether underlying model features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared top-and-random autointerpretability scores for sparse-autoencoder dictionary features with alternative decompositions.
rows.baseline: Default basis, random directions, PCA, and ICA
rows.value: The paper reports sparse-autoencoder dictionary features are far more interpretable by this measure than the alternatives.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals around means are shown in Figure 2; numerical intervals not stated in the text.
rows.note: The text describes the comparison but gives no numerical score values for the plotted comparisons.
rows.check: Figure 2 covers all residual layers, not just early ones. The advantage is largest early. The comparison set includes the default (neuron) basis.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2; Figure 2 caption and following paragraph.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise top-and-random autointerpretability scores for sparse-autoencoder features with alternative decompositions.
rows.value: The paper reports the sparse-autoencoder effect is comparable to ICA in layer 4.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are shown in Figure 2; numerical intervals not stated in the text.
rows.note: The authors say the effect declines through the model and is only comparable to ICA at this layer.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-wise top-and-random autointerpretability scores for sparse-autoencoder features with alternative decompositions.
rows.value: The paper reports minimal improvement in the final layer.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals are shown in Figure 2; numerical intervals not stated in the text.
rows.note: The result limits how broadly the interpretability advantage generalizes across layers.
rows.check: 'Minimal improvement' at the final layer is near-absent. The authors attribute it partly to autointerpretation limits rather than SAE failure.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Recomputed autointerpretability scores using only randomly selected fragments.
rows.value: The paper reports learned features still consistently outperform baselines, especially in early layers; random-only scores are substantially smaller than top-and-random scores.
rows.note: The text describes the direction of the comparison but does not provide numerical scores.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M
rows.operation_detail: Patched selected residual-stream dictionary features using counterfactual activations on the IOI task.

conditions.value: sparse; trained on first 10,000 elements of the Pile

rows.measure: KL divergence from target against number of patched features
rows.baseline: PCA components and a non-sparse dictionary (α = 0)
rows.value: The paper reports sparse dictionary features reach a given level of KL divergence with fewer patches than PCA, and this does not occur with the non-sparse dictionary.
rows.note: The text states the qualitative result; exact plotted values are not given.

rows.subject: Pythia-410M
rows.operation_detail: Patched selected residual-stream dictionary features using counterfactual activations on the IOI task.
rows.measure: Mean edit magnitude against KL divergence from target
rows.value: The paper reports sparse dictionaries improve the Pareto frontier: comparable editing is achieved with smaller edit magnitude.
rows.note: The text describes the result qualitatively; exact plotted values are not given.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Ablated a dictionary feature identified as activating for apostrophes.
rows.value: Ablation mainly reduces the logit for the following “s” token; the paper says this is the largest decrease.
rows.note: This is a qualitative causal case study of one selected feature, not a broad evaluation of feature recovery.
rows.check: This is a hand-selected single feature (search procedure in Appendix D.3). It illustrates the result but is not a rate.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated language-model perplexity after replacing a layer's residual-stream activations with their sparse-autoencoder reconstruction.
rows.note: The reconstruction loses information and changes model predictions; the paper says the dictionaries do not achieve zero reconstruction loss.
rows.check: Bears on completeness only. Perplexity rises from 25 to 40, so the dictionary is incomplete.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Varied the sparsity coefficient and measured sparsity and reconstruction accuracy.
rows.measure: Average number of active features and proportion of unexplained variance
rows.value: The paper reports a smooth sparsity–accuracy tradeoff and no distinct bump or knee.
rows.note: The authors say this is evidence that there is not one uniquely correct sparse decomposition, while noting more experiments would be needed to confirm it.
rows.check: Bears on canonicity. The authors explicitly hedge: confirming it 'would require many additional experiments'. This is not a direct test of uniqueness.

rows.subject: Pythia-70M
rows.operation_detail: Assessed whether sparse-autoencoder features in MLP activations were active enough to form an overcomplete basis and be automatically interpreted.

conditions.value: twice as many features as neurons

rows.measure: Number of active/interpretable features relative to dictionary size
rows.value: The paper reports that in some cases less than half of the features are active enough for automatic interpretability, so the living features do not form an overcomplete basis.
rows.note: The authors also report mixed success in MLPs and say the training pipeline does not robustly learn overcomplete bases in intermediate MLP layers.
rows.check: Applies to middle and later MLP layers. Early MLP layers have mostly active features. The wording 'less than half might be active' is illustrative, not a measured count.

relationships.condition: Pythia-70M residual stream (especially early layers) and Pythia-410M layer-11 IOI patching
relationships.reason: SAE features beat neuron basis, random, PCA and ICA on autointerp, also under random-only scoring. They localise IOI with fewer, smaller patches than PCA or a non-sparse dictionary (R1, R4, R5, R6, R7).
relationships.display_finding: SAE features scored higher than neuron-basis, random, PCA and ICA directions on autointerpretability, including under random-only scoring. In Pythia-410M they localized IOI with fewer, smaller patches than PCA or a non-sparse dictionary.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Pythia-70M residual stream (especially early layers) and Pythia-410M layer-11 IOI patching
source_check.reason: R1 and R4 show improved interpretation, including random-only scoring; R5–R6 show finer causal localisation. R7 supplies a selected causal example.

relationships.condition: Later residual layers and middle/later MLP layers
relationships.reason: The advantage falls to parity with ICA at layer 4 and is minimal at the final layer. MLP dictionaries lose many features to dead units and are not robustly overcomplete (R2, R3, R10).
relationships.display_finding: The advantage over ICA fell to parity at layer 4 and was minimal at the final layer, and MLP dictionaries lost many features to dead units and were not robustly overcomplete.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Later residual layers and middle/later MLP layers
source_check.reason: R2–R3 show weaker interpretation advantages later; R10 documents mixed MLP recovery with many dead features. These qualify the method's demonstrated reach.

relationships.condition: The tested SAE dictionaries (tied weights, L1 penalty)
relationships.reason: Reconstruction raises layer-2 perplexity from 25 to 40, so the dictionaries are incomplete. A smooth sparsity–accuracy curve with no knee is offered as tentative evidence against a unique decomposition (R8, R9, R10).
relationships.display_finding: Reconstruction raised layer-2 perplexity from 25 to 40, and a smooth sparsity–accuracy curve with no knee was offered as tentative evidence against a unique decomposition.

source_check.reason: Section 6.2 explicitly establishes incomplete reconstruction and a layer-2 perplexity increase from 25 to 40. Appendix B offers tentative evidence against a unique decomposition; stability is untested.

relation.reason: Its own interpretation comparisons, interventions, and reconstruction results bear on V4 and V5.

tranche.reason: Tests recoverable sparse features in pretrained language-model activations, extending the toy-model setting with interpretation and causal-intervention results.

source_check.notes: R10's less-than-half example is illustrative, not a measured rate. Minimal final-layer improvement supports a partial state; the authors also identify limitations of automatic interpretation.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Residual-stream features in early layers and the reported IOI patching experiment
reader_labels.reason: Sparse-autoencoder features score above comparison decompositions in early layers and localise IOI behaviour with fewer patches and smaller edits (R1, R5, R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Later residual-stream layers and middle/later MLP layers
reader_labels.reason: The interpretability advantage shrinks to parity with ICA at layer 4 and minimal improvement in the final layer; many MLP features are inactive and may not form an overcomplete basis (R2, R3, R10).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: The tested sparse-autoencoder reconstructions and sparsity settings
reader_labels.reason: Reconstructions lose information, and the reported smooth sparsity–accuracy tradeoff is presented as evidence against one uniquely correct decomposition; feature stability is not tested (R8, R9).
